o.s: AWOL stands for Addictive Way of Life. The business was incorporated in August 2006 and trades from 190 Harvard Avenue in Allston with a second door at 110 Merrimack Street in Lowell, selling sneakers and streetwear alongside its own print studio. Its own copy describes the shop as a family and a playground for streetwear enthusiasts rather than a store, and it runs raffles for limited sneaker releases.
o.d: Second door of the same operator; see the row for Allston, MA. No founder is named in any source found. Searched Boston Globe, Boston Magazine, BU Today, Hypebeast, Sneaker Freaker, Complex, state and BBB registration records; the corporate filing gives the entity name but no principal. The registered alternate name is Ttp Trading Company, Inc.

o.s: Charlie Davidson was 22 in 1948 when he and his brother-in-law Virgil Marson opened The Andover Shop at 127 Main Street in Andover, in a building Davidson's father Leon already owned and had run clothing and food businesses out of. Davidson was an Andover native and the grandson of Armenian immigrants; Marson was an Armenian immigrant himself. Five years later Davidson opened a second shop at 22 Holyoke Street in Harvard Square, in a building he designed, and the two men split the business between them, Marson running Andover and Davidson running Cambridge. Davidson built the shop around the Ivy League look just as it took hold, and the Cambridge room became a cultural salon as much as a store, drawing Miles Davis, Chet Baker, Bobby Short, Ralph Ellison and Albert Murray. He worked there almost until his death in 2019 at 93. The Mscisz family, longtime customers, bought the business in 2018.
o.w: Charlie Davidson and Virgil Marson (founders); Mscisz family since 2018
o.d: Jack Lemmon worked the Andover sales floor as a Phillips Academy graduate and later shopped there as a Harvard student. Davidson's role is the subject of an oral history, Miles, Chet, Ralph & Charlie, published 2024.

o.s: Oliver Mak, Jay Gordon and Dan Natola were working odd creative jobs in Boston in the early 2000s: Mak was DJing, promoting parties and running a non-profit finding paid art work for teenagers, Gordon shared an office with him downtown, and Natola came in through the Floorlords b-boy crew. They wanted a clubhouse for the projects nobody in the city would fund, and opened Bodega in 2006 behind the front of a working corner store, reachable through a door disguised as a vending machine. Nike granted the shop tier-zero access within two years and the collaborations followed; a house apparel line launched in 2012 and a replica store opened in Tokyo in 2014.
o.w: Oliver Mak; Jay Gordon; Dan Natola
o.d: Mak has described the corner-store front as a metaphor for the business: not everyone needs imported Japanese clothing but everyone needs toilet paper.

o.s: Lloyd Anderson, a Seattle transit worker and climber, could not find a decent ice axe in the United States at a price he could afford, so in the mid-1930s he ordered one direct from Austria for a few dollars. His wife Mary read and spoke German and placed the orders. Friends from The Mountaineers club wanted the same deal, so in June 1938 the Andersons and a group of fellow climbers formed a cooperative, each paying a dollar for lifetime membership. The first shop was a shelf in a grocery store, then three shelves at the back of a filling station; the Andersons took no pay for eight years. The co-op now runs well over a hundred stores, of which the Boston branch on Brighton Avenue is one.
o.d: Not an independent stockist: this is a branch of a member-owned national cooperative with roughly 23 founding members.

o.s: Sneaker Junkies opened in 2007 on Weybosset Street in downtown Providence, selling limited-release sneakers, streetwear and accessories, and later moved to Thayer Street. It expanded to 268 Newbury Street in Boston in late 2014 and added a New Haven store on Chapel Street. The business has stayed in the limited-release and collaboration end of the trade across all three doors, including an adidas Gazelle made with the shop in 2026.
o.d: No founder is named in any source found; searched Boston Magazine, GoLocalProv, Providence Journal coverage, the shop's own blog and a university case study. Live-status flag for the register: the shop's own social bio marks the Boston door as currently closed, and recent release posts list only Providence and New Haven.

o.s: Isadore Katz began as a peddler serving immigrant families who could not make themselves understood in English shops and were mocked for it. On 11 March 1947 he opened Miltons in Quincy with his sons Nathan and Milton, naming it for one of them. The business ran three Quincy stores at one point before consolidating into shopping-centre locations. Milton's son Dana ticketed stock in the warehouse as a boy and travelled to New York on buying trips with his father, became a buyer in 1983 and chief executive in 1991. The company expanded its Chestnut Hill Square store in 2013 and opened a third door at the Burlington Mall in 2022, each running over 10,000 square feet of menswear and boyswear.
o.w: Isadore Katz with sons Nathan and Milton; now Dana Katz
o.d: Three generations: Isadore, Milton and now Dana Katz. Sources vary on the founders' names, with one directory rendering them as Isadore Milton and Nathan Katz rather than three men.

f: Miltons The Store For Men — Braintree, MA

o.s: Gary Drinkwater came up through visual merchandising and then spent formative years at Louis Boston under Murray Pearlstein, travelling with him on buying trips; he also met his wife Teresa Borges there. When he told a mentor in 2003 that he wanted to open a tailored menswear store, the reply was that he must be out of his mind, because menswear was weak and tailoring weaker. They shook hands on it anyway, and by August 2004 Drinkwater and Borges had opened in Porter Square, in the Henderson Carriage Repository, a five-storey brick building the Henderson brothers rebuilt in 1892 to store and show carriages. During the 2008 downturn and again through the Covid closures, customers bought large gift certificates simply to keep the shop trading.
o.d: It is the only store in America authorised to repair Paraboot shoes, and its made-to-measure shirt programme has ranked sixth worldwide by units.

o.s: Michael opened his first store, Eskil's Clog Shop, in Boston at 24, selling Swedish clogs. In 1979 he opened Northern Pursuit, a ski shop in Killington, Vermont, and grew to five stores over the next three years, arranging his life around skiing in the New England mountains through winter and water sports on Martha's Vineyard through summer. Island Pursuit followed as the coastal counterpart to the ski shops, on Martha's Vineyard in 1983 and Nantucket in 1985. By the late 1980s, with two young daughters, he decided an endless summer was easier to manage than snowsuits and mittens, and the business moved toward the coast. Island Pursuit now trades in Sarasota and Sanibel in Florida, Chatham, Newport and Mystic.
o.d: Operator link for the register: the Chatham MA and Newport RI rows are the same business, which also runs doors in Mystic CT and two in Florida. Only the founder's first name is given in the company's own account.

o.s: Puritan traces to a small clothing and shoe store on Main Street in Plymouth in 1919. Abraham Penn, then 22, ran the shoe department; when the founder died two years later Penn and a new partner, Achille Maccaferri, bought the business from the estate for four thousand dollars. They took the name to Cape Cod, opening on Main Street in Chatham in 1925 with Penn's distant cousin Ben Shufro as manager, a post he held for 41 years. Harwich Port followed, then Hyannis in 1939, which became the headquarters and later moved to 408 Main Street. Penn's sons Milton and Howard came in as boys filling orders; the third generation, cousins Rick and Jim, joined in the 1980s and widened the store beyond menswear. There are now four Cape stores, a private chino label started in 2012 and a restaurant, cafe and spa inside the Hyannis flagship.
o.w: Abraham Penn; sons Milton and Howard Penn; now Rick Penn and Jim Penn
o.d: Sources conflict on the founding: Puritan's own account says Abraham Penn opened the first store in 1919, while a local history says Sam Levine opened it and hired Penn, who bought it from Levine's estate in 1921. Penn's line was that he would rather make a friend than make a sale.

o.s: Jeff Blue was a marketing executive at large footwear and apparel companies, and kept hearing the same question at parties and children's soccer games in Boston's western suburbs: where does a man actually buy clothes out here. In 2008 he opened Blue Dry Goods on Walden Street in downtown Concord, selling to men and boys. Kathy Smith joined him in 2010 with a long retail background and an ambition to own a store of her own. Blue offered her the business in 2021, which she had not expected, and she took it on knowing the customers already. She has kept the assortment traditional while adding brands, shoes and accessories.
o.d: The name is the founder's surname rather than a colour or a nod to old dry-goods stores.

o.s: Joseph Gibeley sold hats through the Depression and in 1949 opened a kiosk and then a shop on Washington Street in Salem, stocking felt hats and small accessories. Scarves and gloves followed, then menswear. His son Robert joined in 1951, by which time the business traded under the shortened surname. In the 1970s the family opened a second store at the Liberty Tree Mall in Danvers and closed Salem, and in 1997 left the mall for a freestanding site on Route 114. Alan Gibeley, the third generation, now runs an 11,000 square foot store; his sister Alison leads a growing womenswear department. Tailored clothing still accounts for about half of sales.
o.w: Joseph Gibeley (founder); Robert Gibeley; now Alan Gibeley
o.d: Giblees bought the Boston haberdasher Zareh in 2018, and MR Magazine named it North American specialty menswear retailer of the year in 2024.

o.s: Husband-and-wife co-owners opened Dune on Winter Street in Edgartown in April 2024, aiming at a gap they felt the Island had carried for years: a men's shop stocking everything from beach clothes to a suit for a summer wedding. Kiersted grew up on Martha's Vineyard, spent over a decade in advertising in Los Angeles, and returned at the start of the pandemic to the family business, The Boneyard.
o.d: The founding brief was that a man should be able to lose his suitcase and replace everything he needs in one store.

o.s: North River Outfitter opened in 2006 as a single shop on the corner of Charles and Revere streets in Boston and grew alongside its customers into the places they spend their summers, adding doors on Nantucket, Martha's Vineyard and in Wellesley. The buy is built around established coastal and preppy labels including Barbour, Peter Millar, Vilebrequin, Patagonia, Tory Burch and Kate Spade, and the store positions itself around New England sophistication rather than a single category.
o.d: No founder is named in any source found; searched the Boston Globe, Boston Magazine, Vineyard Gazette, MV Times, Inquirer and Mirror, and trade press. Queue note: the same operator runs doors on Nantucket, in Wellesley and on Charles Street in Boston, none of which appears in the register.

o.s: Shoe Market began in 1998 in Cohasset and has grown to multiple doors on the South Shore: the main store at Derby Street Shoppes and an outlet at Lincoln Plaza, both in Hingham. It has traded at Derby Street since the centre opened in 2004 and marked its twentieth year there in 2024. Staff include family and friends who have been in the shoe business since 1980.
o.d: The store's stated philosophy is that big things happen in small stores. Derby Street Shoppes is a WS Development property, so this stockist is already a WS tenant.

o.s: The Arcadian Shop started in 1974 on Church Street in Lenox, founded by Larry Lane with his friend John Fernsall on the idea of turning a love of the outdoors into a living. It moved to Williamstown and back to Lenox, settling at 91 Pittsfield Road in a building dating to the late eighteenth century, on the edge of the 400-acre Kennedy Park, which puts a trailhead at its front door. Lane became sole owner in 1982 and ran it for four decades, watching the outdoor trade consolidate from small operators into corporate hands around him. In 2022 he sold to three longtime employees, all Berkshire County natives who had each worked there at least 25 years.
o.w: Larry Lane and John Fernsall (founders); Chris Calvert, Keith Dupuis and Jeff Minkler since 2022
o.d: Sources give the building as 1791 and 1781, and the sale as 2022 and 2023. The shop runs community events including weekly summer paddleboard socials at Stockbridge Bowl.

o.s: Mel and Enid Zuckerman founded Canyon Ranch in Tucson in the late 1970s after Mel turned his own health around and decided to build a resort around the idea. Looking to expand, they bought Bellefontaine in Lenox in 1987 for six million dollars. The mansion, built in the late 1890s and modelled on the Petit Trianon at Versailles, had been a private house, a seminary and a boys' boarding school, then stood empty and was damaged by fire. Rather than build a modern compound the Zuckermans restored the mansion and added New England-style buildings around it, opening on 1 October 1989 with an inn, a large spa and an integrative health centre on about 120 acres.
o.ot: Subsidiary of Canyon Ranch, privately held
o.d: Not a stockist in the ordinary sense: this is a destination wellness resort with a retail shop attached, so any brand list attached to this row reflects a resort boutique rather than a specialty store.

o.s: AWOL stands for Addictive Way of Life. The business was incorporated in August 2006 and trades from 190 Harvard Avenue in Allston with a second door at 110 Merrimack Street in Lowell, selling sneakers and streetwear alongside its own print studio. Its own copy describes the shop as a family and a playground for streetwear enthusiasts rather than a store, and it runs raffles for limited sneaker releases.
o.d: Second door of the same operator; see the row for Allston, MA. No founder is named in any source found. Searched Boston Globe, Boston Magazine, BU Today, Hypebeast, Sneaker Freaker, Complex, state and BBB registration records; the corporate filing gives the entity name but no principal. The registered alternate name is Ttp Trading Company, Inc.

o.s: Cara first came to Nantucket in 2003 at nineteen and spent her summers there, then made the island her home, raising a family and working in retail for more than two decades. She opened her own boutique at 12A Oak Street in 2025, aimed at what she saw as a gap for a shop balancing elegance with clothes people can actually live in on the island. It carries both men's and women's brands, among them Rhône, Lem Lem, Rowan, Stillwater and Madeleine Thompson.
o.d: One of the few genuinely mixed men's and women's openings in the queue; most recent island arrivals are womenswear only.

o.s: The shop began as the Toggery Shop at 62 Main Street in 1916, successor to a Nantucket store the Genesky family had run since 1908. Philip Genesky hired Philip Murray Jr. to manage it; Murray had been working in retail since he was fourteen and gave up scallop fishing to take the job. He bought the store in 1945, borrowing from his brother Herbert, who ran a package store, and renamed it. He kept it open year-round on the reasoning that islanders need shirts and shoes in winter too. His son Philip C. Murray came back from Virginia in the early 1950s, bought the neighbouring Louis Coffin Dry Goods store in 1963 to add a women's department, and in the same decade introduced a red canvas trouser meant to fade with washing and sea air. Nantucket Reds were trademarked in 1980 as their reputation spread. John Murray and Trish Bridier, the third generation, took over in 2000.
o.w: Philip Murray Jr. (bought the store); Philip C. Murray; now John Murray and Trish Murray Bridier
o.d: The red canvas was modelled on the tanned sails of Brittany fishing boats. The Official Preppy Handbook named the store the island outfitter, which is what turned a local shop into a national one. Murray's and Sylvia Antiques are Nantucket's two longest-running businesses.

o.s: The Nantucket Boat Basin Authentic Shop is the marina's own retail store, selling wearables, headwear and accessories carrying Boat Basin and Nantucket branding to visitors, boaters and islanders. It trades from 33 Straight Wharf on Nantucket alongside the marina operation rather than as a standalone clothing business.
o.d: Register correction: this shop is at 33 Straight Wharf, Nantucket MA 02554, not Stoughton MA 02072. It is also a marina-branded merchandise shop rather than a multi-brand stockist, which changes how any brand list on the row should be read. No founding date or named founder was found.

f: Nantucket Boat Basin Authentic Shop — Nantucket, MA

o.s: The Haul Over has outfitted Nantucket since 1995 from the corner of Salem and Candle Streets, near the boat docks, on the premise that the island's weather turns fast enough that visitors and residents both need proper outdoor clothing rather than resort wear. Owners Mike Campbell and Greg Donoghue built it around outdoor and casual island brands for the whole family, and it became one of New England's largest single-store Patagonia dealers. It stays open all year except February and March.
o.d: The name refers to a narrow spit of beach on the island's northeast side where fishermen once dragged their boats out of the harbour and hauled them over the sand to reach the fishing grounds east of the island.

o.s: Simon & Sons sells clothing for men and boys and has been a family business through three generations. It traded on Needham Street in Newton for roughly two decades before moving in 2013 to a former party-supply shop at 679 Highland Avenue in Needham, taking about half as much space again as it had before; the fit-out was designed to keep a traditional feel in a modern room. Suiting, tailoring and rentals for boys and young men are a substantial part of the trade.
o.f: unknown (trading in Newton by the early 1990s)
o.d: No founder is named and no founding date is reported in any source found. Searched the Boston Globe, Boston Magazine, Needham and Newton Patch, chamber listings and the contractor's published case study; the case study confirms three generations but names nobody.

o.s: NOT FOUND
o.d: Searched the Newburyport Daily News, Boston Globe North, the Greater Newburyport Chamber, regional press and general web; no founder, date or founding account was found. The door is confirmed at 7 Liberty Street, Newburyport through the johnnie-O dealer list. Spectrum note: this makes four Newburyport rows in the register, of which this is the only one that presents as men's.

o.s: NOT FOUND
o.d: Searched the Newburyport Daily News, the Greater Newburyport Chamber directory, regional press and general web; no founder, date or founding account was found. The shop is confirmed at 58 Merrimac Street selling coastal-themed clothing for women and men alongside accessories, decor, jewellery and work by local artists. The chamber lists a Haverhill mailing address, which may indicate the owner or the registered business sits outside Newburyport.

o.s: Ira Segel opened Mr. Sid in Newton Centre in 1967. His son Stuart was studying for the law boards in 1989 when Ira opened a second store in Palm Beach and needed someone to run it; Stuart took the job instead of sitting the exam and stayed. Barry went to TJX first for a taste of corporate retail and joined in 1996. The Palm Beach lease ended in 2004 and the brothers consolidated back to Massachusetts, later adding a Seaport door. In 2019 they launched Sidney, a made-to-measure line cut for both men and women, with the former Hugo Boss chief executive Barry Wishnow consulting; Wishnow had worked the Mr. Sid floor as a Newton teenager.
o.w: Ira Segel (founder); now Stuart Segel and Barry Segel
o.d: Sources disagree on generation: the store's own writing calls the brothers third-generation clothiers while trade press calls them the second generation to run the business. Note for the register: the row has no zip; the Newton Centre store is 1211 Centre Street, 02459.

o.s: Mosher's has sold men's clothing on Centre Street in Newton Centre since 1921 and is run by the third generation of the founding family. It works across ready-to-wear suiting, custom-made shirts and tailored suits, and does its own alterations, positioning itself on nearly a century of accumulated fitting experience rather than on breadth of stock.
o.d: Spectrum note: Mosher's at 1221 Centre Street and Mr. Sid at 1211 Centre Street are ten doors apart on the same block, two family-owned men's stores founded 46 years apart. No founder's given name is reported in any source found.

f: Mosher's Men's Store — Newton Centre, MA

o.s: Jackson & Connor opened in Northampton in 2007 and trades on the second floor at 150 Main Street, in the Thornes Marketplace building. It sells menswear across a wide price range from more than sixty lines, Canadian, Italian and American, with a full tailoring service that is free on full-price goods and a strong wardrobe-building and styling trade. The room is fitted out more like a lounge than a shop floor, with a pool table, a tin ceiling and leather seating.
o.d: The owner is consistently referred to as Will in customer accounts and local reviews, but no surname or founding narrative appears in any reported source; searched the Daily Hampshire Gazette, the Valley Advocate, MassLive, Northampton chamber listings and trade press.

o.s: Natale Agostino was born in Reggio Calabria and arrived in Massachusetts in 1971 at sixteen, with a fifth-grade education and, by his own account, a dollar and thirty-eight cents. He learned English and learned the trade working for three clothing stores, then opened his own tailor shop in Weymouth Landing at nineteen. To draw people in he put his sewing machine in the window and stitched the same jacket sleeve over and over where passers-by could watch. He moved into selling suits in East Braintree, built a store in Hanover in 1994, and later opened in Norwell. The store carries no outside labels: he travels to Italy and has his own garments made from Zegna, Loro Piana, Vitale Barberis and similar cloth, with free alterations for the life of the garment.
o.d: The store's own account is internally inconsistent on dates, placing the Weymouth Landing shop at age nineteen but the East Braintree expansion in 1973; the founding year here is inferred from his stated age and arrival date. A business directory gives 2012, which is likely the Norwell entity rather than the business.

o.s: NOT FOUND
o.d: Searched the Cape Cod Times, Cape Cod Chronicle, Cape Cod Life, Cape & Plymouth Business, the Orleans Chamber and general web; no founder, date or founding account was found. The door is confirmed at 34-A Main Street, Orleans through the johnnie-O dealer list, which is also how it entered the register. No store site was located. Levi's, Carhartt and Tommy Bahama confirmed on the floor by Sebastian, 23 Sep 2026.

o.s: NOT FOUND
o.d: Searched Provincetown Independent and Banner coverage, the Provincetown Chamber, Cape Cod press and general web. Every result for this name returns Clove & Creek, a home goods and gifts mercantile on Broadway in the Rondout in Kingston, New York, founded by two business partners; nothing was found for a Provincetown store. Register flag: this looks like the same misfiling pattern as HAPPY ON MAIN, where an out-of-state business has been given a local address. Confirm the Provincetown door exists before researching further.

o.s: Brendan Carter grew up in City Point, South Boston, where his parents have lived on East Sixth Street for more than forty years, and the store takes its name from the neighbourhood. He played basketball at BC High and Framingham State, graduated in 2011, coached at Framingham State and Salem State, and in 2012 started a club programme called Rise Above Basketball. Everything he wanted to wear meant a long drive to buy, and after seeing a men's clothing pop-up in New Jersey he opened The Point Clothing Lounge at 135 Emerson Street in late 2022. It is built as a room rather than a shop floor, with drinks, a television and a playable arcade machine, stocking direct-to-consumer labels that had not previously been carried in stores. A second door has since opened at MarketStreet Lynnfield.
o.d: Second door of the same operator; see the row for South Boston, MA. Carter's stated reason for the layout was that department stores left him feeling claustrophobic and overwhelmed.

o.s: NOT FOUND
o.d: Searched MassLive and the Springfield Republican, the Springfield Regional Chamber, Western Mass business press and general web; nothing was found for a Springfield store under this name. Worth confirming the door exists and is currently trading before further research.

o.s: Elaine Barse grew up in Connecticut, read English literature at Smith and moved to Martha's Vineyard after graduating in 1988 without a firm plan. She waited tables and sold advertising for the Vineyard Gazette before finding her way to Peck's Bad Boy, Neil Peck's skate and surf shop, where Peck introduced her to skating and surfing. When he wanted out she could not raise the money to buy him out, so she worked another year, took a job managing LeRoux Clothing to learn retail properly and save, and opened The Green Room in a small space on Spring Street in 1994. She bought LeRoux itself in 2003 and moved to 71 Main Street, which put clothing and surf and skate under one roof, and later opened a dedicated shoe store a few doors down at 65 Main. Patagonia is consistently her best-selling line.
o.d: The name is a surfing term for the few seconds spent inside the barrel of a wave. This is one of the two Vineyard Haven doors the origin brief flagged as missing from the queue; the register now carries it.

o.s: Cai-Cai Fritzinger was building a house north of Boston and working with a British decorator who designed her own fabrics. She wanted to sell pillows made from them, and had just put a copper roof on a shed in the yard, which gave her a product, a place and a name at once. The shed became a store on Main Street in Wenham and later a second location in Manchester-by-the-Sea. The buy is largely European and largely found on her own travels.
o.d: Scope flag for the register: the shop describes its Wenham assortment as a women's collection. Customers looking for the original shed occasionally still turn up in her garden.

o.s: Ann and Dick Squire were both born and raised in Westport and settled there to bring up their three sons. Looking for a business of their own, Dick noticed in the winter of 1977 that a former barn at 842 Main Road appeared empty because there were no tracks in the snowy driveway. They bought the building that year and opened Country Woolens as a sweater and yarn shop, fitting it out with ceiling beams salvaged from a barn in Fall River and adopting a sheep as the logo. An addition went on in 1987; the yarn eventually went and outdoor and casual brands came in. In January 2025, after 47 years, Ann handed the business to her son and daughter-in-law, Ben and Liz Squire, who had worked alongside her for eleven years.
o.w: Ann Squire and Dick Squire (founders); Ben Squire and Liz Squire since 2025
o.d: The 1987 extension was built backwards rather than sideways to avoid felling a maple that still stands by the north door. Register flag: the two Westport rows are one business at 842 Main Road.

o.s: Max Schneider, known as Jimmy, was a professional boxer and a bodyguard and driver for an older entrepreneur named Jaffrey, who gave him his Army Navy store in return for the loyalty. Schneider bought 990 Main Street in Bridgeport in 1920 for three hundred dollars, with an eighth-grade education behind him, and quit the ring to run it. Bridgeport was a manufacturing city then and the shop clothed its working men in overalls, chambray shirts and work boots. It stayed a working man's store until the 1960s, when Jimmy's son Bob came in and began following the trade rather than the factories: bowling slacks, then bell-bottoms, then disco, and from the early 1980s hip-hop, with Shell Toe adidas, Nike and Air Jordans on the wall by 1985. Bob's son Dave is the third generation. The company has run doors in downtown Bridgeport, north Bridgeport, West Haven, Hamden and New Haven.
o.w: Max 'Jimmy' Schneider (founder); Bob Schneider; Dave Schneider
o.d: Sources differ slightly on the address, giving both 990 and 1000 Main Street, which is consistent with a move within the block. The Hamden door is listed as closed. Jimmy's was among the first stores in Connecticut to carry Russell Simmons's line, and dates its best years to roughly 1980 to 2000, before hip-hop retail moved into malls.

o.s: Stephen Zangrillo was 22 and just back from the South Pacific with the Army when his father suggested he open a store. He did, on 1 August 1946, a single room selling sporting goods just down the Post Road from where the business stands now. Known locally as Mr. Z, he ran it on the principle that customers treated like old friends come back, and expanded it steadily from team sporting goods into a 40,000 square foot, three-storey store selling clothing for men, women and children alongside sporting equipment. His daughter Gina Zangrillo is president and has run it for years, with a staff of around fifty and a long record of local philanthropy. The town marked the store's 75th anniversary in 2021 with a Darien Sport Shop Day.
o.d: Register flag: the two Darien rows are the same store at 1127 Post Road; the second is a misspelling, Dariend Sport Shop, and carries a different subtype.

o.s: Jim D'Alessio had managed at Henry Miller in Hartford and run the men's department at Polo Ralph Lauren in Farmington before opening J. Alden in a small space in Essex Village in 1993, then moving to a larger site on Main Street as the trade grew. He and Amy Wilson had been friends since Franklin Pierce University in the 1980s and reconnected years later. In January 2020 a fire at the neighbouring Black Seal restaurant filled the shop with smoke and forced a month of cleaning and repainting; they reopened that spring under the theme of refresh and renew, and launched a women's arm run by Amy. Jim's argument for the store is that the Connecticut shoreline has almost no men's clothing between New Haven and Hartford, and what there is skews ultra-casual outdoor.
o.w: Jim D'Alessio and Amy Wilson D'Alessio
o.d: He still writes receipts by hand, and does fittings at customers' houses. The store also takes in outside alterations, shoe repair and reweaving.

o.s: Richards was an 8,000 square foot privately owned men's store on Greenwich Avenue when Mitchells bought it in 1995, at the time the leading menswear shop in the town. In 2000 the Mitchells reopened it in a 27,000 square foot two-storey building, putting womenswear, designer boutiques, shoes and handbags upstairs and menswear, jewellery and a large coffee bar downstairs. The coffee bar became a meeting place in its own right and the building has won several retail design awards. Tyler Mitchell, of the third generation, runs it now.
o.w: Mitchell family; Tyler Mitchell leads Richards
o.ot: Independent, family-owned; part of Mitchells Stores
o.d: Operator link for the register: this is the same company as the two Mitchells rows in Westport, not an independent Greenwich store.

o.s: Mickey Yardis was 24 in 1979 when he was shown a small newly vacant shop on East Putnam Avenue and took it on the spot. He had read Lehigh, run a sports shop in Danbury afterwards, and been a distance runner in college, so when the running boom arrived he had both the interest and the knowledge to fit people properly. The store has stayed in the same spot on the Post Road ever since, selling running, fitness and outdoor-adventure clothing and footwear, and became a family business with his son working alongside him. Michael Yardis bought it around 2018 and reported the best month in the store's history in December 2022, more than forty years in.
o.w: Mickey Yardis (founder); Michael Yardis (owner since about 2018)
o.d: The shop sponsors local races, including the Jingle Bell Jog, and has outlasted almost every other retailer on that stretch of the Post Road.

o.s: Three partners named Stackpole, Moore and Tryon founded the store in downtown Hartford in 1909, in a building on Asylum Street whose cast-iron Beaux Arts front dates to an 1896 renovation and is on the National Register. Ron Morneault is a lifelong Hartford resident who has worked in downtown retail since he was sixteen. Jody took a part-time job at Westfarms Mall without intending a career in it, became the first woman to sell menswear at Langley's, and Ron later recruited her to work for him. They bought Stackpole Moore Tryon around 2007 and kept its emphasis on quality on the founders' original reasoning that people remember who sold them something good. The store has since moved to a smaller room at 257 Asylum Street, a few steps from its historic corner, refocused on personalised menswear and custom tailoring.
o.w: Stackpole, Moore and Tryon (founders); Ron Morneault and Jody Morneault
o.d: The Morneaults have run their own Hartford retail businesses for over fifty years between them, and are heavily involved in downtown civic work. Sources give the founding as both 1908 and 1909; the store's own material says over a century without settling the year.

f: Morneault's Stackpole Moore Tryon — Hartford, CT

o.s: Ashok Ramchandani founded Ramani's Clothiers and the business has stayed in his family, with three Connecticut stores each run by one of his sons. Custom suits and shirts are the core of it, made to a customer's specifications through the founder's Hong Kong connections, alongside a ready-to-wear buy that differs store to store rather than being held in common.
o.w: Ashok Ramchandani (founder); sons run the individual stores
o.d: Queue additions for the register: the same family runs Ramani's stores in Waterbury and Middletown, neither of which appears in the register. No founding date was reported; the single source found is a commercial listicle rather than reported press, so this row is weak until someone calls the store.

o.s: Two young men in their twenties wanted a store where customers would end up feeling like family, and what their budget allowed was a barn building in Chappaqua, New York, where they opened in 1970 selling jeans and tops. They moved into the village centre before long, widened the buy and opened a second door in New Canaan, Connecticut in 1977. Rick Buggee and Barry Mishkin have run it as co-owners ever since, across roughly 10,000 square feet of men's and women's clothing with tailoring, staying open late and going to customers' houses for fittings when needed. Mishkin describes the floor as theatre and the owners' job as hosting.
o.d: Status flag for the register: the New Canaan door closed in 2024, leaving Chappaqua as the only location. Mishkin has dressed customers including Bill Clinton, who is colour-blind and relied on the store to coordinate.

o.s: Enson's has traded in New Haven since 1924 and has remained in the Enson family across roughly a century, combining tailoring with a buy drawn from a range of international makers.
o.d: No founder's given name, no founding account and no reported press coverage was found; searched the New Haven Register, New Haven Independent, Connecticut Magazine, the Shops at Yale directory and trade press. The date and family continuity come from a commercial listicle and should be treated as unconfirmed.

o.s: Vincent Ferrucci was born in Gioia Sannitica in Italy and began studying tailoring at thirteen, moving to Rome at sixteen to finish his apprenticeship. At twenty he emigrated to Maracaibo in Venezuela, worked two years for a Venezuelan tailor and then opened his own shop there. He arrived in the United States in 1958 as a tourist and stayed, marrying the following year. After working for a series of custom clothiers he opened his own custom tailoring business in 1963 in the Westville section of New Haven. His son joined in 1989 and now runs it from Elm Street, keeping the custom work while adding ready-to-wear.
o.d: Register note: this door settled the Ferrucci test in the affirmative, cutting cloth and stocking brands both, and gave the rule its name.

o.s: Tom Maloney opened Raggs on the day after Thanksgiving in 1984 in Westville, in the northern part of New Haven, with the modest ambition of lasting until Christmas. The original idea was to sell to both men and women. The Westville shop ran until 1988, when he moved to 1020 Chapel Street downtown and the focus narrowed to menswear, built around modern suiting, tailored separates, denim, footwear and accessories, with same-day and next-day alterations. He has run it for more than forty years.
o.d: Register flag: the two New Haven rows, Raggs and Raggs for Men and Women, are the same store at 1020 Chapel Street; the longer name is how the Shops at Yale directory lists it.

o.s: Kelley Frey came out of fashion retail and opened a men's shop in Old Greenwich after concluding that the husbands of her women customers had nowhere convenient to buy clothes. The store sells upscale casual menswear and accessories from a range of vendors and is fitted out as a room men will linger in, with sport on the television, a putting green and games.
o.d: Register flag: the business styles itself Gray Clothier, singular, where the row reads Gray Clothiers. No founding date and no reported press coverage was found; searched Greenwich Time, Greenwich Free Press, Fairfield County press, chamber listings and trade press. The account here rests on a business data profile rather than an interview.

o.s: The Backer family opened the store in New Haven in 1933 with the aim of selling high-quality men's clothing with personal service attached. It traded there for more than sixty years before the family moved the whole shop to Orange in 1996 to sit closer to where its customers had gone, and it now trades from Boston Post Road. The buy runs from tailored clothing through denim, and the store also does tuxedo rental.
o.d: The move was a relocation rather than an expansion: the New Haven store closed when Orange opened.

o.s: NOT FOUND
o.d: Searched the Ridgefield Press, Hamlet Hub, Daily Voice, running trade press and general web; no founder, date or founding account was found. Register flag: the stockist string appears to be two business names concatenated, CT Run Co. and Ridgefield Running Company, which suggests either a rebrand or an acquisition that was captured mid-change. Establishing which came first would settle the row.

o.s: Zahner's is a family-owned men's clothing store and tailor shop on the Hartford Turnpike in Vernon, run by Scott Zahner. It works as a one-stop men's store: ready-to-wear alongside made-to-measure suits, sports coats and trousers produced through Samuelsohn and Heritage Gold, Coppley, and a private-label factory making garments exclusive to the shop, with an on-site tailor doing alterations. It carries Alden and Samuel Hubbard footwear and will take appointments at a customer's office or home.
o.d: Sources give two different foundings and they cannot both be right: the store's own site and listings say 1908, while its LinkedIn profile says the shop opened in 1951 and was started by two brothers. One customer account dates their own patronage to 1961. The 1908 date is the store's most consistent public claim and is used here, with the conflict recorded rather than resolved.

o.s: Daswani Clothiers opened in West Hartford in 1977 and has become one of the area's established men's clothing destinations, working through one-to-one consultation rather than self-service, and offering tailoring on garments bought elsewhere as well as its own.
o.d: No founder is named in any source found; searched the Hartford Courant, We-Ha, Connecticut Magazine, the West Hartford Chamber and trade press. The register notes a mill-or-brand question on Lanificio Colombo at this door, resolved toward stocked via Marc Allen.

o.s: ASF Sports & Outdoors has traded on Post Road East in Westport since 1986 as a family-owned athletic and casual footwear, apparel and equipment store serving Fairfield County. It stocks running, sport, cleat and specialty footwear alongside technical outerwear, and runs a custom embroidery and printing operation called the ASF Logo Wearhouse for teams, schools and companies.
o.d: No founder is named in any source found; searched the Westport News, Westport Journal, Daily Voice, Fairfield County press, chamber listings and trade press. The date and family ownership come from the store's own account.

o.s: Ed Mitchell was 53 in 1958 when he and his wife Norma took over an 800 square foot former plumbing supply office in Westport and opened a men's store with a handful of suit styles at sixty-five dollars each. Norma brought her coffee pot in each day so customers would feel at home. Their son Bill joined full time in 1965 and his brother Jack followed; the store outgrew two locations before settling into its present 17,000 square foot site and changing its name from Ed Mitchells to Mitchells. The company bought Richards of Greenwich in 1995, rebuilt it as a 27,000 square foot store with womenswear in 2000, then acquired Marshs in Huntington in 2006 and Wilkes Bashford in San Francisco and Palo Alto in 2009. It now runs ten stores under five names with a fourth generation of the family working in them.
o.w: Ed Mitchell and Norma Mitchell (founders); Bob Mitchell and Russ Mitchell (co-CEOs)
o.d: Operator link for the register: Mitchells, Mitchells Westport and Richards in Greenwich are all one company, Mitchells Stores, which also owns Wilkes Bashford, Marios and Stanley Korshak. Jack Mitchell turned the family's service method into a book, Hug Your Customers. Sources differ on whether the opening range was three suit styles or five.

o.s: Solstice trades from beneath the National Hotel on Block Island, selling gifts, accessories, ornaments and jewellery on a seaside theme, including handmade work by New England artisans. It operates alongside two sibling shops, B.I. Tees and True North Outfitters, which share a combined website.
o.d: No founder or founding date is reported in any source found; searched the Block Island Times, the Block Island Chamber, Rhode Island press and general web. Scope flag: this is a gift and accessories shop rather than a clothing stockist, and searches are complicated by an unrelated national sunglasses chain of the same name. Queue note: B.I. Tees and True North Outfitters appear to be the same operator and are not in the register.

o.s: Canterbury's Fine Men's Clothing has dressed Cranston for more than forty-five years under husband-and-wife owners Ronald and Jeanne Garafano. It runs custom clothing alongside a designer buy including Tommy Bahama, Mezlan and Di Bello, with tailoring and alterations done in house and often while the customer waits.
o.d: Register note: this door produced the register's first-ever Samuelsohn dealer confirmation, carrying Samuelsohn and Heritage Gold together, which is the pair that list distinguishes dealer by dealer. The founding year is inferred from a 2022 source describing the business as over 45 years old; the single source found is a commercial listicle rather than reported press.

f: Coast To Country Outfitters — Newport, RI

o.s: Man Overboard is a men's clothing and footwear shop at 198 Bellevue Avenue in Newport, carrying seasonal apparel and accessories.
o.d: NOT FOUND for a founding account. Searched the Newport Daily News, Newport This Week, Rhode Island Monthly, Discover Newport and general web; no founder, date or founding narrative was reported anywhere found. Note the shop sits two doors from Michael Hayes on the same stretch of Bellevue Avenue; whether the two are related was not established either way.

o.s: Michael Hayes was 34 in 1983 when he opened a full-service specialty store on Bellevue Avenue in Newport, on the belief that clothing counts for little without trust, relationships and service behind it. He bought from designers worldwide and aimed at timeless style rather than passing trends, frequently dressing several generations of the same family. The business grew to three doors: the Bellevue Avenue store, a children's shop next door at 206 Bellevue, and a store on Bowen's Wharf. His children Max and Hailey Hayes now lead it, and it passed its fortieth anniversary in 2023.
o.w: Michael Hayes (founder); Max Hayes and Hailey Hayes
o.d: His son has said the founder always held that the business should be enjoyable, and that this is part of why customers return.

o.s: Marc Streisand came to New England from New York with more than twenty years in the trade behind him and built Marc Allen on make, cloth and service rather than breadth of assortment. The business runs custom and made-to-measure alongside a buy of exclusive European luxury labels including Incotex, PT01, Inis Meain, Loro Piana and Maurizio Baldassari, with a team of about ten working as personal clothiers rather than floor staff, each handling individual clients' wardrobes and contributing to the seasonal buy.
o.d: Queue note: the company has traded from Providence, Newport and New York; only the Providence door is in the register. Its Partners page gives the cleanest brand-versus-mill split any source in the register has provided, using a structural heading rather than per-entry markers. No founding date is reported in any source found.

o.s: John Piane was born in 1891 to a first-generation Italian family from Campobasso, and grew up on Manhattan's Lower East Side as the eldest son of six children. He went to Dartmouth, graduating in 1914, and managed the shop then called The College Bookstore before buying it and renaming it the Dartmouth Co-op in 1919, a name reflecting that it was run almost entirely by students. He began importing European skis to the Upper Valley the same year, and by 1932 the Co-op was manufacturing its own ski equipment; during the Second World War it was among the main designers and suppliers of ski gear to the American, Russian and Turkish armies. The Piane family ran it until 1986, when a group of alumni headed by Gene Kohn and Allen Stowe, both class of 1960, bought it.
o.w: John Piane (founder); Gene Kohn and Allen Stowe with a group of alumni since 1986
o.d: Scope flag for the register: the Co-op's current clothing is exclusively Dartmouth logo product, which is why its subtype is collegiate. Every universe row on this door should carry the collegiate-programme note so nobody sizes it as a full-line stockist. Not to be confused with the Hanover Consumer Cooperative Society, an unrelated grocery co-op founded in 1936 in the same town.

o.s: The Hubert family started the business in 1972. When Mr. and Mrs. Hubert retired in 1985 their elder son Guenter took it on, and he and his wife Kathy Begin ran it as Hubert's Family Outfitters, joined soon after by Kathy's sister Linda, who brought a background in law and accounting. Guenter's brother Tom came back from Philadelphia as their father's health failed. The three opened a second store in Claremont in 1990 with Tom managing it, then New London in 1991, Lebanon in 1998 and Peterborough in 2008, all served from a central warehouse in Newport. Guenter and Kathy retired in 2017 and Tom and his wife Stephanie now run it with their four children.
o.w: Mr. and Mrs. Hubert (founders); Guenter Hubert and Kathy Begin; now Tom Hubert and Stephanie Hubert
o.d: This door established 1998. Five New Hampshire doors under one family; the register carries them as Claremont, Lebanon, New London, Newport and Peterborough. Newport is the warehouse town as well as a store.

o.s: Kennebunk Outfitters trades from Western Avenue in Kennebunk's Lower Village, selling custom casual pieces of its own alongside outside labels including Wanakome and Coast Hippie. A regional shopping guide describes it as a second-generation family business that opened in 1977.
o.d: Attribution caution: the 1977 founding and the second-generation description come from a list-format shopping guide where each description sits between two entries, so the attribution is probable from the layout rather than certain. Treat the date as unconfirmed until someone checks with the store. No founder is named in any source found; searched the Portland Press Herald, York County Coast Star, Mainebiz and the Kennebunk-Kennebunkport chamber.

o.s: Dannah for Men is a men's shop in Kennebunkport carrying gifts, home decor, barware, books, personal care and grooming, wallets, watches, belts, hats, sunglasses and apparel, with stock that turns over continuously. It presents itself as the town's newest men's store and reads as a men's offshoot of an established local retail name.
o.d: No founder, founding date or founding account is reported in any source found; searched the Portland Press Herald, Kennebunk Post, Seacoast press, the Kennebunkport Chamber and general web. Apparel is one category among many here rather than the core of the business.

o.s: Philip Adams, known as Bing, bought the Kittery Trading Post on Route 1 from Frank Haskell in 1938 for four thousand dollars. It was then a one-room building with gas pumps. He built a reputation as an honest horse trader, swapping fur pelts for petrol, beef for ammunition and supplies for a car, and drew customers from a long way off on that basis. The pumps are long gone and the store now runs to about 90,000 square feet across hunting, fishing, camping, water and winter sports, clothing and footwear, with an enclosed boatyard. It was named Maine retailer of the year in 2001.
o.d: Register flags: the store's own About page is now served from allgeargroup.com, which suggests a group or ownership structure worth confirming. An unreliable listing gives the founding as 1912, which is the trading post's own age rather than the Adams family's tenure; 1938 is the acquisition date.
o.sn: Kittery Trading Post (own copy via listing)

o.s: David Hodgkins spent eight years learning the trade and building contacts before opening David Wood Clothiers in Falmouth in 1978. Wood is his mother's maiden name; he chose it partly to please her and partly because it looked better on a sign than his own. He aimed at customers who wanted classic styling at a fair price. The store moved to Portland in the mid-1980s, at Market and Middle streets, and to Commercial Street in 2011. Hodgkins met Sara Hutchison Brown, who had spent years on the wholesale side of luxury menswear mostly for Italian brands and regarded him as a mentor, at a New York show in 2016 and asked her to move to Portland and eventually take over. She relocated the following year and took the business on when he retired.
o.w: David Hodgkins (founder); Sara Hutchison Brown since 2023
o.d: The store has carried Alden of New England for decades, and Alden makes styles exclusively for it.

o.s: Dylan John and his fiancee Ellen opened Fore & Wharf on Fore Street in Portland's Old Port in July 2023, selling men's and women's clothing with a coastal New England slant alongside skincare and fragrance. John worked through the business plan, seasonal inventory and financial projections with a Maine Small Business Development Center advisor before opening, and has since built collaborations with local brands into the assortment.
o.w: Dylan John and Ellen (surname not reported)
o.d: Founded on the back of a formal business plan written with a state small-business advisor rather than a lease taken on instinct.

o.s: Joseph Redman grew up in Portland's West End, graduated from Bowdoin in 1970 and finished an MBA in 1974. His thesis argued for a specialty menswear store in a market that had none, and that autumn he found a newly restored warehouse in the Old Port and opened Joseph's at 410 Fore Street. The store has traded from the same address ever since and is the city's oldest men's clothing store.
o.d: He wrote his MBA thesis on opening a retail clothing store and then opened one within months of graduating.

o.s: Lazy Sun began in Park City, Utah, as an outdoor apparel and lifestyle shop. Maine native Jordan Haddadi and her husband Mark Pomykato moved the business east and reopened at 28 Exchange Street in Portland's Old Port over Memorial Day weekend 2025, choosing the city for their family home as well as the store. The buy mixes Japanese and Korean labels with American workwear-influenced house product designed with a Los Angeles team.
o.d: The Portland opening was a relocation rather than a second door, and the couple moved their household with the business.

o.s: Peter Renney's Fashions is a family retail business on Exchange Street in Portland's Old Port, built around hand-tailored suits, custom shirts, coats and trousers alongside related clothing, and sold with individual attention rather than off a rail. Its buy has run to Coppley, Keithmoor, Jack Lipson, Dion neckwear, cloth by Ermenegildo Zegna, Kolte, Martin Dingman and Johnston & Murphy.
o.d: No founder or founding date is reported in any source found; searched the Portland Press Herald, Mainebiz, Maine Magazine, Portland Old Port and Portland Downtown listings and trade press. Live-status flag for the register: the shop's own social page has carried a 'Closing Soon' marker; the door is on the register's visit list and this is worth confirming on the same trip.

o.s: Stewart and Marianne Smith saw that the midcoast had no local outdoor retailer and opened Maine Sport Outfitters in 1976 as a small neighbourhood shop in downtown Camden, starting in athletic apparel and moving quickly into outdoor clothing and equipment. After several years of growth they built a purpose-designed flagship on Route 1 in Rockport in 1990. When sea kayaking took off along the Maine coast in the late 1980s and early 1990s they recognised what was happening and built an Outdoor School around it, with a lodge on Gay Island to host trips, which turned the business into part retailer and part guide service. The Rockport store has been expanded twice since. Camden reopened after closing in the late 1990s, and a Rockland store opened in the renovated former Sears and Roebuck building on the corner of Main Street. The company marked fifty years in 2026.
o.d: The Rockport flagship, purpose-built in 1990. Still owned by its founders half a century on, and a member of the Grassroots Outdoor Alliance.

o.s: MK Clothing trades on Burlington's Church Street Marketplace. In August 2026 it was bought by McNeil & Reedy, the Rutland menswear store founded in 1956 by James F. McNeil and George Reedy and now run by third-generation owner Casey McNeil. MK keeps its own name and its own staff under the new ownership; it is McNeil & Reedy's first location outside Rutland.
o.d: Operator link for the register: same company as the McNeil & Reedy row in Rutland. No founding date or founder for MK itself under its previous ownership was reported in any source found.

o.s: Russ Scully built WND&WVS as a garage brand first, pressing his own logo onto t-shirts for friends. After being asked to test paddleboards for a New York Times piece in 2009 he became the local point of contact for anyone wanting to buy one, and for a couple of years sold boards out of The Spot, the surf-themed restaurant he and his wife Roxanne run on Shelburne Road. They opened the shop in a renovated 3,000 square foot space on Pine Street in Burlington's South End, and own the building. The business has since grown to include the Burlington Surf Club on Lake Champlain.
o.d: Sources report the shop opened in December but do not give the year; 2013 is inferred from the couple's move to Burlington around 2012.

o.s: James F. McNeil and George Reedy both worked at the Economy, the department store next door on Merchants Row that was Vermont's largest retailer in the 1950s, and left to open their own men's shop in 1956. McNeil had started at the Economy as an elevator operator. His sons Jim and John ran the store for more than fifty years before passing it to Casey McNeil, the third generation. It is the oldest continuously operated retail business in downtown Rutland, and about a quarter of its trade comes from weddings.
o.w: James F. McNeil and George Reedy; now Casey McNeil (third generation)
o.d: In August 2026 McNeil & Reedy bought MK Clothing on Burlington's Church Street Marketplace, its first location outside Rutland; MK keeps its own name and staff.

o.s: Chris and Taice Perrotti lived for a few years on Archery Close, a small dead-end street in Connaught Village, London, with their young daughters, and named the business after it. Taice opened the womenswear store first; Chris opened Archery Close Men's above it in December 2022, on the second floor of 25 Main Street in Stowe village, on the grounds that the town had good women's boutiques and outdoor shops but nothing comparable for men. He buys smaller labels chosen for quality rather than name recognition, among them Faherty and Billy Reid.
o.d: The logo is a London Underground roundel pierced by an arrow, drawn with Stowe designer Sally Stetson. Note for the register: both stores now trade from 1650 Mountain Road, not 25 Main Street.

o.s: Lenny's Shoe & Apparel has outfitted working people and families in Vermont since 1990, built around work footwear, work clothing and outdoor gear rather than fashion, and carrying Carhartt, KEEN, Bogs, Dansko, Timberland Pro, Chippewa, Kuhl and the Vermont-made Darn Tough alongside a general family clothing selection. It has run an annual sock drive with Darn Tough for fifteen consecutive years, giving thousands of pairs to neighbours in need.
o.d: No founder is named in any source found; searched Seven Days, VTDigger, the Burlington Free Press, Vermont Business Magazine and trade press. Register note: this is one operator across four doors (Williston, Barre, St. Albans in Vermont and Plattsburgh in New York), so its brand list should not be counted four times.

o.s: Woodstock Sports trades from 30 Central Street in Woodstock village, selling sporting and outdoor goods alongside apparel and footwear. Its own site leads with a line attributed to Benjamin Franklin about the bitterness of poor quality outlasting the sweetness of a low price, which is the whole of its stated positioning.
o.d: No founder, founding date or founding account is reported in any source found; searched the Vermont Standard, Seven Days, VTDigger, the Woodstock Area Chamber and general web. Register note: this door's logo wall was dated by filename timestamps as roughly two-thirds October 2018, so its captured brand list should be treated as stale until refreshed.

o.s: Mark Goldfarb and Tom Fagan were colleagues with decades in the menswear trade between them when they founded Mark Thomas in Albany in 2004, taking the name from their own first names. The store sells traditional and contemporary tailored clothing with Canali from Italy and Jack Victor from Montreal at its centre, alongside sportswear, shoes and formalwear, and runs made-to-measure programmes through Canali, Jack Victor, Mel Gambert and Individualized Shirts with fitting and tailoring done on site. Its core trade is men who wear suits for work, and long-standing customers who bring their sons in for a first suit. A second store has since opened on Broadway in Saratoga Springs.
o.d: Queue addition for the register: the Saratoga Springs door is not in the register. Sources give the partners' combined experience as both forty and fifty years, in listings written years apart.

f: Mark Thomas Men's Apparel — Albany, NY
Southampton Blazer And Button Co. — Garden City, NY

o.s: Antonio D'Agostino started in Larchmont as a custom tailor, working out of a small store on Palmer Avenue. He outgrew it and moved to larger premises on the Boston Post Road, outgrew that too, and ended up in his own building at 138 Larchmont Avenue. His sons Erminio and Tony run it now as a men's and boys' clothing store with tailoring done on the premises by three tailors and a seamstress, covering everything from bar mitzvahs and communions to weddings and proms, and taking in women's alterations as well. Antonio died in 2021; a photograph of him and his wife hangs at the back of the shop.
o.w: Antonio D'Agostino (founder); sons Erminio D'Agostino and Tony D'Agostino
o.d: Sources give the founding as both 1962 and 1964, the latter usually tied to Antonio starting as a tailor on Palmer Avenue; both dates appear in the store's own material. Visitors are offered a free espresso.

o.s: Two brothers, Murray and Lee Levitt, opened Mur-Lee's in Lynbrook in 1946, taking the name from their own first names. The second generation, Bruce and Harry, run it now, with Bruce's wife Judy handling the social side. It trades from about 4,500 square feet on Atlantic Avenue selling men's and boys' clothing, custom suits and shirts and shoes, and has three generations of customers on its books. Bruce puts the store's recent strength down to having moved into sportswear early rather than staying tailored-only.
o.w: Murray Levitt and Lee Levitt (brothers); now Bruce Levitt and Harry Levitt
o.d: The store passed 75 years in 2021 and has won a Long Island Choice award for best men's and boys' clothing store; its history has been recorded in a StoryCorps interview with Bruce Levitt.

o.s: Harry Rothman was 15 in 1918 when his father was struck and killed by a horse-drawn ice wagon on the Lower East Side, leaving him as the eldest of eight to support the family. He left school and sold rags from a pushcart on Delancey Street. In 1926 he and his brother opened Harry Rothman's in a small Bleecker Street shop, buying excess stock from good manufacturers and selling it cheap, which effectively invented the discount clothing store. The business moved several times and settled near Fifth Avenue and 18th Street, running close to sixty years. It closed when Harry died in 1985. His grandson Ken Giddon was trading bonds in Boston and about to start at MIT Sloan when the family asked him to help liquidate it; he went to New York for what he expected to be two weeks, reopened the store in Union Square in 1986 instead, and his brother Jim joined a few years later. It shifted over time from discounter to full-price and added stores in Scarsdale in 1999 and Bronxville.
o.w: Harry Rothman (founder); Ken Giddon and Jim Giddon
o.d: Harry's standing instruction to staff was to keep a sense of humour, on the grounds that they were not curing anyone, only selling trousers. The business marked its centenary in 2026.

o.s: Thomas F. Finnigan had spent twelve years with the clothiers C. J. Carey Co. and knew most of Saranac Lake by the time he opened his own men's store at 78-80 Main Street in 1923, with a modern shopfront designed by a New York specialist. He later bought the whole building and enlarged it. His son Thomas F. Finnigan Jr. started at eleven as a delivery boy, worked up through the company, served as president and retired in 1985. Thomas F. Finnigan III ran it for the next 35 years. In August 2018, after several years of looking for a buyer who would keep both the business and the building intact, he sold to Jimmy and Johnny Williams, brothers born and raised in Saranac Lake who had returned home and opened a bar and restaurant on Broadway. The custom interior woodwork is original.
o.w: Thomas F. Finnigan (founder); three generations of Finnigans; Jimmy Williams and Johnny Williams since 2018
o.ot: Independent; sold out of the founding family in 2018
o.d: Ownership flag for the register: the store left the Finnigan family in 2018 after 95 years and three generations, though the name and the fittings stayed. The family name may run six or seven generations deep, with a connection to the linen markets of County Cork.

f: T.F. Finnigan, Inc — Saranac Lake, NY

o.s: Jim Foley spent the first 24 years of his career working for Thomas Miller at Miller's Woodbury store. When Miller retired and sold the business to Mitchells, the team moved on to Marsh's, but their Woodbury customers had nowhere to follow them to. In 2012, the week Hurricane Sandy hit, Foley and his partners opened a new shop half a mile down the road from where they had started. It runs to about 2,200 square feet, keeps two full-time tailors, and is built on relationships and on a buy of exclusive luxury makers including Fedeli, Luciano Barbera, Etro, Stenstroms, Belvest, Gran Sasso and Paul & Shark.
o.w: Jim Foley, Rich O'Boyle and Amir Moradi
o.d: Operator context for the register: this shop exists because of a Mitchells acquisition. Miller's store went to Mitchells, and Marsh's, where the team landed next, is also a Mitchells store — the same company as the Mitchells row in Huntington and the three Connecticut rows.

o.s: Louis LaRossa came from Potenza in southern Italy and founded LaRossa Shoe in 1923; the repair business has traded in the Boston area ever since, passing to his son William and now to Gina and William LaRossa. LOUIE is the clothing shop the family added beside it in the LaRossa Building on Columbian Square, selling sportswear, outerwear and footwear for men and women. In 2025 the LaRossas opened LOUIE for Him inside Henry's Shoe Repair at 104 North Street, Hingham, a men's-only door carrying Alden, Herno, Lardini, Ring Jacket and Barbour.
o.w: Louis LaRossa (founder); Gina and William LaRossa
o.d: Brand list read from the house's own Brands menu on louiestyle.com, 15 September 2026, which mixes men's and women's labels; the shop carries an own label, LOUIE / LaRossa. Mon–Fri 10–5, Sat 10–4.

o.s: Puritan Cape Cod is a third-generation family clothier, opened by Abraham Penn in 1919 and run today by his grandsons Richard and James Penn. The Hyannis flagship at 408 Main Street has traded since May 1939, in the former post office of the 1928 Public Service Building, and carries a full in-house tailor shop, made-to-measure suiting and casual coastal clothing; a cafe adjoins it and a day spa sits beneath. Four stores across the Cape.
o.w: Abraham Penn (founder); Richard and James Penn
o.d: flagship. Brand list carried over from the Chatham record, which was read from puritancapecod.com; the chain merchandises as one.
o.sn: St. Johns featured retail partners; hmdb.org marker for 408 Main St
